chapter_note.about: Fractions, ratios and percentages are the language of probability and of the General Aptitude section. This chapter rebuilds seven tools from zero: fractions, fraction arithmetic, ratios and weighted averages, proportion and rates, percentages, percentage change, and compound growth. Each card starts with a picture you can sketch in the margin of the exam paper and ends with a question shaped like GATE. The aim is speed without slips, because these are marks you should never lose.
chapter_note.simple: A fraction says how many equal slices you have out of how many the whole was cut into. A ratio says how many parts of one thing go with how many parts of another. A percentage is a fraction out of 100. Almost every problem here asks the same question: what part of what? Percentages are taken from the number you start with, so a rise followed by an equal fall does not bring you back. Growth that builds on itself, like interest on interest, multiplies each time instead of adding.

cards.title: Fractions: parts of a whole
cards.simple: A fraction says how many slices you hold out of how many equal slices the whole was cut into. Picture a chocolate bar with 4 equal pieces: eat 3 and you have eaten $\frac34$. Cut the same bar into 8 pieces and you must eat 6 to eat the same amount, so $\frac34=\frac68$. The bottom number is the size of the slices and the top number is how many you hold. To compare two fractions, cut both into slices of the same size and count them. In exam words: equal fractions come from multiplying top and bottom by the same number, and you compare fractions over a common denominator.
cards.idea: A fraction is a part of one whole, cut into equal slices. The **bottom** number says how many equal slices make the whole. The **top** number says how many you take. Cutting every slice smaller changes the numbers but not the amount, so $\frac34$, $\frac68$ and $\frac9{12}$ are all the same value.
cards.definition:
$$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{a\cdot k}{b\cdot k}\qquad(b\ne0,\ k\ne0)$$

$a$ is the numerator (how many slices you take), $b$ is the denominator (how many equal slices make one whole), and $k$ is any number you multiply or divide both by. To **simplify**, divide top and bottom by their biggest common factor. To **compare** $\frac ab$ and $\frac cd$ with positive bottoms, cross-multiply: $\frac ab>\frac cd$ exactly when $ad>cb$.
cards.intuition_full: Picture two identical strips of paper. Cut one into 4 slices and the other into 8, then shade the same length on both. The first strip has 3 slices shaded, the second has 6. The shaded length is the same, but the count differs because the slices are half the size. That is why multiplying top and bottom by the same number never changes the value: the count and the slice size move in opposite directions. Comparing uses the same trick. $\frac35$ and $\frac47$ are hard to compare because the slices differ. Cut both into 35ths: $\frac{21}{35}$ and $\frac{20}{35}$, and now you just count. Cross-multiplying does this without writing the 35ths: $3\times7=21$ against $4\times5=20$, so $\frac35$ is bigger. A fraction can also be larger than 1, such as $\frac74$, which is one whole plus $\frac34$.

examples.setup: Show that $\frac34=\frac68=\frac9{12}$ with three strips, then simplify $\frac9{12}$ back.
steps: Cut a strip into 4 equal slices and shade 3. That is $\frac34$.
Cut an identical strip into 8 slices. The same shaded length covers 6 slices, so it is $\frac68=\frac{3\times2}{4\times2}$.
Cut a third strip into 12 slices. The same length covers 9, so it is $\frac9{12}=\frac{3\times3}{4\times3}$.
The three shaded bars end at the same line. Equal fractions come from multiplying top and bottom by the same number.
Backwards (simplifying): divide top and bottom of $\frac9{12}$ by 3 to get $\frac34$.

examples.setup: Arrange $\frac57$, $\frac7{10}$ and $\frac23$ from smallest to largest.
steps: The bottoms are 7, 10 and 3. No two share a factor, so the common bottom is $7\times10\times3=210$.
$\frac57=\frac{5\times30}{7\times30}=\frac{150}{210}$.
$\frac23=\frac{2\times70}{3\times70}=\frac{140}{210}$.
Over equal slices, compare the tops: $140<147<150$. Check with decimals: $0.667<0.700<0.714$.
examples.answer: $\frac23<\frac7{10}<\frac57$. The trap avoided: judging by how big the numbers look instead of by the value.

examples.setup: Which is larger, $-\frac12$ or $-\frac13$? And write $\frac74$ as a mixed number.
steps: Ignore the signs first: $\frac12>\frac13$, since halves are bigger slices than thirds.
On the number line, $-\frac12$ sits further left of zero than $-\frac13$.
Further left means smaller, so $-\frac12<-\frac13$. A bigger size behind a minus sign gives a smaller number.
$\frac74$: 4 goes into 7 once with 3 left over, so $\frac74=1\frac34$.
examples.answer: $-\frac13$ is larger, and $\frac74=1\frac34$ (a fraction can exceed 1).

cards.why: Fractions are how every probability is written and how most aptitude data is given. If you cannot move between $\frac34$, $\frac68$ and $0.75$ quickly, every later chapter slows down. In GATE: ranking probabilities, reducing an answer to lowest terms for a NAT, and comparing ratios in aptitude data.
how: To compare, put both over a common bottom or cross-multiply.
To simplify, divide top and bottom by the same factor until nothing more divides both.
To change the bottom, multiply the top by the same number as the bottom.
Sanity-check with a decimal, or against the landmarks $\frac12$ and 1.
cards.mistake: Thinking a bigger bottom number means a bigger fraction, or adding the same number to top and bottom. $\frac18$ is smaller than $\frac15$ because eighths are smaller slices. And $\frac{3+9}{5+9}=\frac{12}{14}$ is not $\frac35$. Only multiplying or dividing both by the same number keeps the value.
edge_cases: Zero on top: $\frac0b=0$ for any $b\ne0$.
Zero on the bottom is not allowed: you cannot cut a bar into 0 slices.
Negative fractions flip the order: $-\frac12<-\frac13$.
Top bigger than bottom, such as $\frac74$, means more than one whole.
connections: Used in: Probability. Every probability is a fraction from 0 to 1, and answers like $\frac2{15}$ and $\frac4{30}$ must be recognised as equal.
Used in: General Aptitude. Comparing fractions sits under ratio and data-interpretation questions.

check.q: Simplify $\frac{18}{42}$.
Which is larger: $\frac49$ or $\frac37$?
Write $\frac25$ with bottom 35.
check.a: $35=5\times7$, so multiply the top by 7 too: $\frac{14}{35}$.

cards.title: Adding, multiplying and dividing fractions
cards.simple: Adding fractions is like adding pieces of pizza: you can only add pieces of the same size, so first cut them to match. Multiplying is different. 'Half of a third' means cut a third in half, and the piece you get is one sixth, so $\frac12\times\frac13=\frac16$. To divide by a fraction, ask how many of those pieces fit. How many half-litre cups fit in 3 litres? Six, which is $3\times2$, so dividing by $\frac12$ means multiplying by its flip. In exam words: add over a common denominator, multiply numerators and denominators straight across, and divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
cards.idea: Adding and subtracting need pieces of the **same size**, so match the bottoms first. Multiplying means 'a fraction **of** a fraction', and you multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. Dividing asks 'how many of these fit in that?', and it turns into multiplying by the flipped fraction.
cards.definition:
$$\frac ab\pm\frac cd=\frac{ad\pm cb}{bd},\qquad \frac ab\times\frac cd=\frac{ac}{bd},\qquad \frac ab\div\frac cd=\frac ab\times\frac dc$$

$a,b,c,d$ are whole numbers. Every bottom is non-zero, and for division $c\ne0$ as well. The fraction $\frac dc$ is the **reciprocal** (the flip) of $\frac cd$. In a sum, the new bottom is a common multiple of the old ones. The smallest one (the LCM) keeps the numbers small.
cards.intuition_full: Why must the bottoms match for addition but not for multiplication? Adding counts slices, and you can only count slices of the same size. Multiplying is a different operation: it takes a fraction *of* an amount. Draw a rectangle with 4 rows and 3 columns. Shading 3 rows is $\frac34$. Taking 2 of the 3 columns inside the shaded part keeps $2\times3=6$ cells out of 12, so $\frac23\times\frac34=\frac6{12}$. The tops multiply (cells kept) and the bottoms multiply (cells in total). For division, ask a counting question: how many $\frac18$ fit in $\frac34$? Since $\frac34=\frac68$, the answer is 6. The flip rule agrees: $\frac34\times\frac81=6$. Multiplying by a fraction below 1 makes a number smaller, and dividing by one makes it bigger. A good habit is to cancel before you multiply. In $\frac58\times\frac4{15}$, the 5 and 15 share a factor 5, and the 8 and 4 share a factor 4, so it becomes $\frac12\times\frac13=\frac16$.

examples.setup: Find $\frac23\times\frac34$ using a rectangle.
steps: Cut a rectangle into 4 rows and 3 columns: 12 equal cells.
Shade 3 of the 4 rows. That is $\frac34$ of the rectangle.
Now take 2 of the 3 columns. That is $\frac23$ **of** the shaded part.
The cells inside both outlines: $2\times3=6$ cells, out of 12 in total.
$\frac23\times\frac34=\frac{2\times3}{3\times4}=\frac6{12}=\frac12$.

examples.setup: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A)=\frac13$ and $P(B)=\frac14$. Find $P(A\text{ or }B)$.
steps: For independent events, $P(A\text{ and }B)=\frac13\times\frac14=\frac1{12}$.
The rule for 'or' is $P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\text{ and }B)$.
Put everything over 12: $\frac13=\frac4{12}$ and $\frac14=\frac3{12}$.
Simplify: $\frac6{12}=\frac12$. Check: $1-P(\text{neither})=1-\frac23\times\frac34=1-\frac12=\frac12$.
examples.answer: $P(A\text{ or }B)=\frac12$. The trap avoided: adding $\frac13+\frac14$ and forgetting to subtract the overlap.

examples.setup: Compute $\frac34\div\frac18$ and $\frac18\div\frac34$. Are they equal?
steps: $\frac34\div\frac18=\frac34\times\frac81=\frac{24}{4}=6$. Six eighths fit in three quarters.
$\frac18\div\frac34=\frac18\times\frac43=\frac4{24}=\frac16$.
They are not equal, so order matters in division. Dividing by a fraction below 1 gave a bigger number (6), and dividing by a larger fraction gave a small one ($\frac16$).

cards.why: Probability answers are fractions, and many need an add, a subtract and a multiply in one line. In GATE: independent events, two-draw problems, and 'a fraction of a fraction' stories in aptitude and probability.
how: To add or subtract: find a common bottom (the LCM), rewrite both fractions, combine the tops.
To multiply: cancel common factors across the top and bottom first, then multiply across.
To divide: flip the second fraction and multiply.
Turn mixed numbers into improper fractions before you multiply or divide.
Reduce the final answer to lowest terms.
cards.mistake: Adding tops and bottoms: $\frac12+\frac13=\frac25$. That is smaller than $\frac12$, which cannot happen when you add. The right answer is $\frac36+\frac26=\frac56$. A second slip is flipping the wrong fraction in a division: flip only the one you divide **by**.
edge_cases: Dividing by zero is undefined: $\frac ab\div0$ has no value.
$\frac ab\div\frac ab=1$ for any non-zero fraction.
A mixed number such as $2\frac12$ is $\frac52$ before you multiply or divide.
Multiplying by $\frac12$ halves a number; dividing by $\frac12$ doubles it.
connections: Used in: Probability. $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)P(B)$ for independent events is multiplying fractions, and prob.conditional chains fractions along a tree.
Used in: Algebra. Rational expressions follow the same rules (found.algebra, card 2).
Used in: General Aptitude. Work-and-rate puzzles add fractions of a job per hour.

Multiply $\frac58\times\frac4{15}$.

cards.title: Ratios, shares and weighted averages
cards.simple: A ratio compares two amounts by saying how many parts of one go with how many parts of the other. If you mix paint with 2 cups of blue to 3 cups of white, the ratio is 2 : 3. That recipe has 5 equal parts in all, so blue is $\frac25$ of the mix. To share money in a ratio, find what one part is worth and then count parts. An average works the same way when groups differ in size: a big group counts for more, so you add up all the marks and divide by all the students. In exam words: a ratio $a:b$ splits a total into $a+b$ equal parts, and a weighted average is total value divided by total weight.
cards.idea: A ratio $a:b$ says that for every $a$ parts of one thing there are $b$ parts of another. To use a ratio on a real total, count the **total parts**, find the value of **one part**, then multiply. When groups of different sizes are averaged, each group counts in proportion to its size. This is a **weighted average**.
cards.definition:
$$\text{share}_1=\frac{a}{a+b}\times T,\qquad \text{share}_2=\frac{b}{a+b}\times T$$

$T$ is the total being split and $a+b$ is the number of equal parts. For a weighted average with weights $w_i$ and values $x_i$:

$$\text{average}=\frac{w_1x_1+w_2x_2+\cdots}{w_1+w_2+\cdots}$$

Equal ratios behave like equal fractions: $2:3=4:6$. To chain $A:B$ and $B:C$, scale them so that B is the same number in both.
cards.intuition_full: A ratio is a recipe. '2 cups blue to 3 cups white' works for a tiny jar or a huge bucket, because only the proportions matter. Counting parts turns the recipe into amounts: 5 parts in all, so each part is one fifth of the mixture. Note that $2:3$ is not the fraction $\frac23$. The parts of the whole are $\frac25$ and $\frac35$, because the whole is 5 parts. Now the weighted average. Say 12 students scored 70 on average and 8 scored 85. The mean of 70 and 85 is 77.5, but 12 students outnumber 8, so the true average should sit closer to 70. Weights fix this: the group totals are $12\times70$ and $8\times85$, and there are 20 students altogether. A weighted average always lies between the smallest and largest values, closer to the group with more weight. This 'weights times values' idea comes back as the expected value in probability, where the probabilities are the weights.

examples.setup: Share ₹90 between A and B in the ratio $2:3$.
steps: A gets 2 parts and B gets 3 parts.
Parts in all: $2+3=5$.
One part is worth $90\div5=18$.
A gets $2\times18=36$ and B gets $3\times18=54$.
Check: $36+54=90$, and $36:54$ reduces to $2:3$.

examples.setup: Section P has 12 students with average 70. Section Q has 8 students with average 85. Find the average of all 20 students.
steps: Total marks in P: $12\times70=840$.
Total marks in Q: $8\times85=680$.
All 20 students together: $840+680=1520$.
Average: $1520\div20=76$.
Check: 76 lies between 70 and 85, nearer 70 because P is the bigger group. The plain mean of the two averages, 77.5, would be wrong.
examples.answer: 76. The trap avoided: averaging the averages.

examples.setup: $A:B=2:3$ and $B:C=5:7$. Find $A:B:C$, and find $C$ if $A+B+C=138$.
steps: B is 3 in the first ratio and 5 in the second. Make both equal to $3\times5=15$.
Multiply the first ratio by 5: $A:B=10:15$. Multiply the second by 3: $B:C=15:21$.
One part is $138\div46=3$, so $C=21\times3=63$.

cards.why: Almost every aptitude question about sharing, mixing, or averaging across groups is a ratio question in disguise. The weighted average is the same idea as expected value in probability. In GATE: share-in-a-ratio, ratio chains, class averages and mixture problems.
how: Add the ratio parts to get the total number of parts.
Divide the total by that number to get the value of one part.
Multiply one part by each ratio term.
For chains, scale so the shared term is the same in both ratios.
For averages, add up (weight × value) over all groups, then divide by the total weight.
cards.mistake: Treating $2:3$ as if A is $\frac23$ of the total, or averaging two averages without weights. A is $\frac25$ of the total, because the total is $2+3=5$ parts. And the mean of 70 and 85 is not the overall average unless the two groups are the same size.
edge_cases: A ratio with a zero term, like $0:5$, gives one side nothing.
Ratios are order-sensitive: $2:3$ and $3:2$ are different.
A ratio can compare more than two things, like $3:4:5$.
If all groups have equal size, the weighted average is the plain mean.
connections: Used in: Probability. A weighted average with probabilities as weights is the expected value (prob.rv).
Used in: Probability. Odds of $a:b$ mean a probability of $\frac a{a+b}$.
Used in: General Aptitude. Mixture, partnership and class-average questions.

check.a: 8 parts, each worth 7: the shares are 21 and 35.

cards.title: Proportion and rates
cards.simple: If 5 pens cost ₹60, then 10 pens cost twice as much. That is direct proportion: double one thing and the other doubles too. Now think of painting a wall. If you double the painters, the job takes half the time. That is inverse proportion: one goes up, the other goes down, and painters times days stays the same. A tap that fills a tank in 6 hours fills one sixth of it each hour, and rates like these simply add up. In exam words: direct proportion keeps the ratio constant, inverse proportion keeps the product constant, and rates (job per hour) add.
cards.idea: Two quantities are in **direct proportion** when doubling one doubles the other: their ratio stays fixed. They are in **inverse proportion** when doubling one halves the other: their product stays fixed. Work and speed questions use **rates**, such as 'job per hour', and the rates of machines working together add.
cards.definition:
Direct: $\dfrac yx=k$ is constant, so $y_2=y_1\cdot\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}$.

Inverse: $x\cdot y=k$ is constant, so $y_2=y_1\cdot\dfrac{x_1}{x_2}$.

A job done in $t$ hours has rate $\frac1t$ job per hour. Rates working together add: $\frac1{t_1}+\frac1{t_2}=\frac1t$. **Average speed** is total distance ÷ total time.
cards.intuition_full: Fix the total amount of work as a count of worker-days (or pump-hours). 4 painters for 9 days is 36 painter-days. It is the same 36 whether you spread it over 4 painters or 6, so painters × days stays at 36. That is the whole idea of inverse proportion. Direct proportion is the unit rate: if 5 notebooks cost ₹140, one costs ₹28, so 8 cost $8\times28$. Rates add because they measure the same thing, the share of the job done per hour. If tap A fills $\frac16$ of a tank per hour and tap B fills $\frac1{12}$, together they fill $\frac16+\frac1{12}=\frac14$ per hour, which takes 4 hours. A tap that *empties* has a negative rate. For average speed, speeds are not what adds up: distances and times are. Going 60 km at 40 km/h takes 1.5 h, and coming back at 60 km/h takes 1 h, so the average is $\frac{120}{2.5}=48$, not 50.

examples.setup: 4 painters finish a job in 9 days. How many days do 6 painters need?
steps: Each cell is one painter-day. 4 painters for 9 days make a grid of 4 rows and 9 columns.
Total work: $4\times9=36$ painter-days.
With 6 painters the work is still 36 cells, now arranged in 6 rows.
Columns: $36\div6=6$ days. More painters, fewer days.

examples.setup: A car drives 60 km at 40 km/h and returns the same 60 km at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole trip.
steps: Going: $60\div40=1.5$ hours.
Returning: $60\div60=1$ hour.
Total distance is 120 km and total time is 2.5 hours.
Average speed $=120\div2.5=48$ km/h.
The plain mean $\frac{40+60}2=50$ is wrong because the car spends more time at the slower speed.

examples.setup: Tap A fills an empty tank in 6 hours. Drain B empties a full tank in 9 hours. With both open, how long does the tank take to fill?
steps: Rate of A: $+\frac16$ tank per hour. Rate of B: $-\frac19$.
Net rate: $\frac16-\frac19=\frac3{18}-\frac2{18}=\frac1{18}$ tank per hour.
Time $=1\div\frac1{18}=18$ hours.
If the drain were stronger than the tap, the net rate would be negative and the tank would never fill.

cards.why: Rates and proportion decide whether you scale a time up or down. Choosing direct when the situation is inverse is the most common aptitude mistake. In GATE: work and time, pipes and tanks, speed-distance-time, and unit-rate questions in General Aptitude.
how: Ask: if one quantity doubles, does the other double (direct) or halve (inverse)?
Direct: find the unit rate, then multiply.
Inverse: find the constant product (the total work), then divide.
Rates of jobs: write each as $\frac1{\text{time}}$, add them (subtract for a drain), then invert.
Average speed: total distance over total time, never the mean of the speeds.
cards.mistake: Using direct proportion when the situation is inverse. Fewer workers means *more* days, so the answer must go up. Check the direction of your answer against common sense before you finish.
edge_cases: Work done may not be the whole job. Track the part completed, then the part remaining.
A drain is a negative rate. If it is stronger than the tap, the tank never fills.
Units must match: 40 km/h is not the same as 40 m/s.
Not every pair is proportional: a taxi with a fixed starting fee does not charge in direct proportion to distance.
connections: Used in: General Aptitude. Work, pipes, speed-time-distance.
Used in: Algorithms. Scaling a measured cost to a bigger input is proportional reasoning, which algo.complexity makes precise.
Used in: Probability. Unit rates like 'events per hour' feed the Poisson model (prob.discrete).

check.a: One pen is ₹12, so 8 pens cost $8\times12=96$ rupees, which is ₹96.

cards.what: Two quantities are in **direct proportion** when doubling one doubles the other: their ratio stays fixed. They are in **inverse proportion** when doubling one halves the other: their product stays fixed. Work and speed questions use **rates**, such as 'job per hour', and the rates of machines working together add.
cards.what_full:
Two quantities are in **direct proportion** when doubling one doubles the other: their ratio stays fixed. They are in **inverse proportion** when doubling one halves the other: their product stays fixed. Work and speed questions use **rates**, such as 'job per hour', and the rates of machines working together add.

Direct: $\dfrac yx=k$ is constant, so $y_2=y_1\cdot\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}$.

Inverse: $x\cdot y=k$ is constant, so $y_2=y_1\cdot\dfrac{x_1}{x_2}$.

A job done in $t$ hours has rate $\frac1t$ job per hour. Rates working together add: $\frac1{t_1}+\frac1{t_2}=\frac1t$. **Average speed** is total distance ÷ total time.

**Worked example.** 4 painters finish a job in 9 days. How many days do 6 painters need?

1. Each cell is one painter-day. 4 painters for 9 days make a grid of 4 rows and 9 columns.
2. Total work: $4\times9=36$ painter-days.
3. With 6 painters the work is still 36 cells, now arranged in 6 rows.
4. Columns: $36\div6=6$ days. More painters, fewer days.

**Answer:** 6 days.

cards.title: Percentages
cards.simple: 'Per cent' literally means 'per hundred'. If your phone battery shows 35%, then 35 out of every 100 parts of the battery are full. To find 35% of something, split it into 100 equal parts, take one part, and multiply by 35. To say what percent one number is of another, divide them and multiply by 100. If you scored 18 out of 60, that is $\frac{18}{60}=0.3$, so 30%. In exam words: $x\%$ means $\frac x{100}$, so $x\%$ of $y$ is $\frac x{100}\times y$, and 'what percent is $a$ of $b$' is $\frac ab\times100$.
cards.idea: A percentage is a fraction whose bottom is always 100. So 35% is just $\frac{35}{100}$ or 0.35. To take a percentage **of** an amount, multiply. To ask 'what percent is $a$ of $b$?', divide $a$ by $b$ and then multiply by 100.
cards.definition:
$$x\%=\frac{x}{100},\qquad x\%\text{ of }y=\frac{x}{100}\times y,\qquad a\text{ is }\left(\frac ab\times100\right)\%\text{ of }b$$

$x$ is the percentage, $y$ is the whole, and $a$ is the part you are comparing with the whole $b$. Useful landmarks: 10% is a tenth, 25% is a quarter, 50% is a half, 12.5% is an eighth. Also $x\%$ of $y$ equals $y\%$ of $x$.
cards.intuition_full: Picture a square cut into a 10 by 10 grid. The whole square is 100%, and each small square is 1%. Shading 35 squares is 35%. Now say the whole is 280 instead of 100. The grid is the same, but each small square is now worth $280\div100=2.8$. So 35% of 280 is 35 squares worth 2.8 each, which is 98. The percent tells you how many squares, and the whole tells you how much each is worth. To go the other way ('what percent of 60 is 18?'), ask how many of the 100 squares the 18 would fill. $18\div60=0.3$, so 30 squares, which is 30%. A percent is a fraction in disguise, which is why $x\%$ of $y$ and $y\%$ of $x$ agree: both equal $\frac{xy}{100}$. Percentages above 100 simply mean more than the whole: 150% of 40 is 60. And a percent of a percent multiplies: 40% of 50% is $0.4\times0.5=20\%$.

examples.setup: Find 35% of 280. Then find what percent 18 is of 60.
steps: Percent means out of 100. The 100 squares make the whole, 100%.
35% is 35 squares out of 100, which is $\frac{35}{100}$.
For a whole of 280, one square (1%) is worth $280\div100=2.8$.
Reverse: 18 out of 60 is $\frac{18}{60}=0.30$, which fills 30 squares of 100, so 30%.

examples.setup: A quiz has 50 questions. 40% are maths and the rest are other topics. A student answers 75% of the maths questions and 60% of the other questions correctly. What percentage of all the questions did the student answer correctly?
steps: Maths questions: 40% of 50 $=20$. Other questions: $50-20=30$.
Correct in maths: 75% of 20 $=15$.
Correct in the rest: 60% of 30 $=18$.
Total correct: $15+18=33$ out of 50.
Percentage: $\frac{33}{50}=0.66=66\%$. The plain mean of 75 and 60 would be 67.5, which ignores the different group sizes.

examples.setup: Show that 16% of 25 equals 25% of 16, and find 120% of 50.
steps: 25% of 16 $=\frac{25}{100}\times16=4$. Both equal $\frac{16\times25}{100}$.
120% of 50 $=1.2\times50=60$. A percentage above 100 gives more than the whole.

cards.why: Every data table, discount, error rate and accuracy score in aptitude and ML is a percentage. You need to move between percent, fraction and decimal without thinking. In GATE: percent-of-percent word problems, data interpretation, and accuracy or error figures in machine learning questions.
how: Write the percent as a fraction over 100 (or as a decimal).
"Of" means multiply.
For 'what percent', compute part ÷ whole and multiply by 100.
Use landmarks: 10% (move the point), 50%, 25%, 1%.
For groups of different sizes, work with counts first, then convert back to a percent.
cards.mistake: Averaging percentages of different-sized groups, or dividing by the wrong whole. 75% in maths and 60% elsewhere is not 67.5% overall unless both parts have the same number of questions. Convert to counts first.
edge_cases: 100% of something is the whole, and 0% is nothing.
Percentages can exceed 100%: 150% of 40 is 60.
Percent to decimal: divide by 100. Decimal to percent: multiply by 100.
$x\%$ of $y$ equals $y\%$ of $x$, which helps when one of them is easier.
connections: Used in: Probability. A probability of 0.35 is 35%, and accuracy or error rates in ml.cv and ml.logreg are percentages.
Used in: Probability. Group splits like 'percent of boys who wear glasses' are the first step of the law of total probability (prob.conditional, prob.bayes).
Used in: General Aptitude. Data-interpretation tables.

cards.title: Percentage change
cards.simple: A percentage change tells you how far something moved compared with where it started. If a phone costs 400 and the price rises 15%, you add 15% of 400, which is 60, so it now costs 460. Then the shop cuts 15% off the new price. That is 15% of 460, which is 69, and you land on 391. You are not back at 400. The second 15% was taken from a bigger number, so it removed more than the first one added. In exam words: a rise of $r\%$ multiplies by $1+\frac r{100}$, a fall multiplies by $1-\frac r{100}$, successive changes multiply, and percentage change is (new − old) divided by old.
cards.idea: A percentage change is always measured against the **old** value. A rise of 15% multiplies the old value by 1.15, and a fall of 15% multiplies it by 0.85. Two changes in a row **multiply**, they do not add, so a rise followed by an equal fall does not bring you back.
cards.definition:
$$\text{change}\,\%=\frac{\text{new}-\text{old}}{\text{old}}\times100,\qquad \text{new}=\text{old}\times\left(1\pm\frac r{100}\right)$$

Use $+$ for a rise and $-$ for a fall. Successive changes of $r_1\%$ and $r_2\%$ give the total multiplier $\left(1\pm\frac{r_1}{100}\right)\left(1\pm\frac{r_2}{100}\right)$. To go **backwards**, divide by the multiplier. When a quantity is itself a percentage (a rate going from 8% to 10%), the difference is measured in **percentage points**, and the percent change is the points divided by the old rate.
cards.intuition_full: A multiplier is the cleanest way to think. 'Up 15%' means the new price is 115% of the old one, so multiply by 1.15. 'Down 15%' leaves 85%, so multiply by 0.85. A chain of changes is a chain of multipliers: $400\times1.15\times0.85=391$. Multiplication does not care about order, so a rise then a fall gives the same final price as the fall then the rise, but it only equals the start if the multipliers cancel exactly. To undo a rise of 25%, the multiplier 1.25 must be cancelled by $\frac1{1.25}=0.8$, a fall of 20%. And to undo a fall of 20% you need a rise of 25%. The asymmetry comes from the base changing. Reverse percentages use division in the same way: if the price after a 20% discount is 720, the old price is $720\div0.8=900$. Never add 20% to 720 to 'undo' it. Finally, keep points and percent apart. A rate that goes from 8% to 10% rose 2 percentage points but 25 percent, because $\frac{10-8}{8}=0.25$.

examples.setup: A price of 400 rises by 15%, then the new price falls by 15%. Find the final price and the net change.
steps: Start: 400.
Fall 15% of the new price: 15% of 460 is 69, so $460\times0.85=391$.
Net: $391-400=-9$, which is $\frac{-9}{400}=-2.25\%$. The second 15% was taken from a bigger base.
examples.answer: Final price 391, a net fall of 2.25%.

examples.setup: A price is raised by 20% and then cut by 25%. Find the net percentage change, and the rise needed afterwards to return to the original price.
steps: Multipliers: $1.20$ for the rise and $0.75$ for the cut.
Net multiplier: $1.2\times0.75=0.9$.
The net change is $0.9-1=-0.1$, a fall of 10%.
To return, the multiplier must be $\frac1{0.9}=1.111\ldots$, so a rise of $11.11\%$ (which is $\frac19$).
examples.answer: A net fall of 10%, then a rise of 11.11% to recover. The trap avoided: adding +20 and −25 to get −5.

examples.setup: A bank rate rises from 8% to 10%. Give the change in percentage points and in percent.
steps: Percentage points: $10-8=2$ points.
Percent change: $\frac{10-8}{8}\times100=25\%$.
Both statements are correct, but they are different numbers. Check which one the question asks for.
examples.answer: 2 percentage points, which is a 25% rise.

cards.why: Prices, discounts, growth rates, accuracy changes and 'x% faster' claims are all percentage changes. The multiplier method turns a long story into one line of multiplication. In GATE: successive discounts, reverse percentages, 'by what percent must it fall to undo the rise?', and percent-versus-points traps.
how: Turn each change into a multiplier: $1+r$ for a rise, $1-r$ for a fall.
Multiply the multipliers for successive changes.
Net change is (final multiplier − 1) × 100.
To work backwards, divide by the multiplier.
Say clearly whether the question wants percent or percentage points.
cards.mistake: Adding or cancelling percentages: thinking +20% then −20% is zero, or that a 20% rise and a 25% fall make −5%. The percentages are taken of different bases, so they multiply: $1.2\times0.8=0.96$, a 4% fall.
edge_cases: A fall of 100% leaves 0, and a price cannot fall by more than 100%.
Order does not matter for the final price, because multiplication commutes.
A rise of 100% doubles, and a rise of 200% triples.
Percentage points only make sense for quantities that are already percentages.
connections: Used in: General Aptitude. Discounts, profit-and-loss and growth questions.
Used in: Calculus. Relative change $\frac{\Delta f}{f}$ is the idea behind logarithmic derivatives (found.derivatives).
Used in: Machine Learning. 'Accuracy rose from 92% to 94%' is 2 points, about a 2.2 percent rise.

cards.title: Compound growth and decay
cards.simple: Put ₹100 in a bank that pays 10% a year. After one year you have ₹110. The next year the bank pays 10% on ₹110, not on the original ₹100, so you earn ₹11 instead of ₹10. Your interest earns its own interest, and the growth speeds up like a snowball rolling downhill. Each year you multiply by the same number, 1.10, so after 3 years you have multiplied by $1.10\times1.10\times1.10$. Things that shrink by a fixed percent each year, like a car losing value, work the same way with a multiplier below 1. In exam words: compound growth is $A=P(1+r)^n$, which multiplies each period, unlike simple interest, which adds the same amount each year.
cards.idea: When growth is a **percentage of the current amount**, each period multiplies by the same factor $1+r$. After $n$ periods you have multiplied $n$ times, so $A=P(1+r)^n$. This beats simple interest (adding the same amount each year) because the growth itself grows. A fixed percentage fall works the same way with a factor below 1.
cards.definition:
$$A=P\left(1+\frac{R}{100}\right)^n$$

$P$ is the starting amount, $R$ is the percentage growth **per period**, $n$ is the number of periods, and $A$ is the amount after $n$ periods. Simple interest is only $A=P\left(1+\frac{Rn}{100}\right)$. For a fall of $R\%$ per period (depreciation), use $1-\frac R{100}$. The **doubling time** is the smallest $n$ with $\left(1+\frac R{100}\right)^n\ge2$, roughly $72\div R$ periods.
cards.intuition_full: Take ₹5000 at 8%. Year 1 adds 8% of 5000, which is 400. Year 2 adds 8% of 5400, which is 432. Year 3 adds 8% of 5832, which is 466.56. The yearly addition keeps growing because the base keeps growing. Simple interest would add 400 every year and reach 6200. Compounding reaches 6298.56, and the difference of 98.56 is interest earned on interest. The shortcut is to multiply by 1.08 three times, or once by $1.08^3$. Depreciation is the mirror image. Losing 10% a year is a multiplier of 0.9, so after 7 years you keep $0.9^7\approx0.478$ of the value. That is a loss of about 52%, not 70%. The rule of 72 gives a quick check for doubling time: at 12% a year it says 6 years, while the exact answer needs the first whole $n$ with $1.12^n>2$, which is 7. Compound growth is the stepwise cousin of the exponential $e^{rt}$ in found.explog, and the yearly balances form a geometric sequence (found.series).

examples.setup: ₹5000 grows at 8% compound interest per year. Find the amount after 3 years and compare it with simple interest.
steps: In one line: $5000\times1.08^3=6298.56$. Simple interest gives $5000+3\times400=6200$, so the extra 98.56 is interest on interest.

examples.setup: Money grows at 12% per year, compounded annually. After how many whole years does it first more than double?
steps: We need the smallest $n$ with $1.12^n>2$.
$1.12^6\approx1.9738$, still below 2.
So 7 years. The rule of 72 says $72\div12=6$, a close estimate that is slightly short.

examples.setup: A machine loses 10% of its value every year. What fraction of its value is left after 7 years, and what percent has been lost?
steps: Each year multiplies the value by $0.9$.
After 7 years: $0.9^7\approx0.4783$.
Not 70%: each year's 10% is taken from a smaller value.
examples.answer: About 47.8% is left, so about 52.2% is lost.

cards.why: Compounding is how money, populations, data and running times grow. It is the bridge to $e$, logarithms and geometric series. In GATE: compound interest and growth word problems, doubling time, and exponential recurrences such as $T(n)=2T(n-1)$.
how: Write the per-period multiplier: $1+r$ for growth, $1-r$ for decay.
Raise it to the number of periods and multiply by the starting amount.
For doubling or other targets, try successive powers until you cross the target.
Compare with simple interest by adding the same amount each period.
Check that a compound answer is above the simple-interest value.
cards.mistake: Using simple interest where the question says compound, or adding the percentages (20% for 5 years is not 100%). Growth in year 2 is a percentage of the year 1 total, so use a power, not the product of $n$ and $r$.
edge_cases: One period: compound and simple interest agree.
Growth rate 0%: nothing changes, because the multiplier is 1.
Fractional periods (half a year) need a fractional power, which is where logs come in.
Decay never reaches zero: $0.9^n>0$ for every $n$.
connections: Used in: Calculus. $\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n\to e$ is the limit of ever more frequent compounding (found.limits_intuition, found.explog).
Used in: Series. Yearly balances form a geometric sequence, and their sum is a geometric series (found.series).
Used in: Algorithms. $T(n)=2T(n-1)$ doubles at every step, which is compounding at 100% (dm.recurrence, algo.complexity).

$P$ is the starting amount, $R$ is the percentage growth **per period**, $n$ is the number of periods, and $A$ is the amount after $n$ periods. Simple interest is only $A=P\left(1+\frac{Rn}{100}\right)$. For a fall of $R\%$ per period (depreciation), use $1-\frac R{100}$. The **doubling time** is the smallest $n$ with $\left(1+\frac R{100}\right)^n\ge2$, roughly $72\div R$ periods.

**Worked example.** ₹5000 grows at 8% compound interest per year. Find the amount after 3 years and compare it with simple interest.

1. Year 0: ₹5000.
2. Year 1: 8% of 5000 is 400, so $5000\times1.08=5400$.
3. Year 2: $5400\times1.08=5832$.
4. Year 3: $5832\times1.08=6298.56$.
5. In one line: $5000\times1.08^3=6298.56$. Simple interest gives $5000+3\times400=6200$, so the extra 98.56 is interest on interest.

**Answer:** ₹6298.56 compound, against ₹6200 simple.
cards.why_full:
Compounding is how money, populations, data and running times grow. It is the bridge to $e$, logarithms and geometric series. In GATE: compound interest and growth word problems, doubling time, and exponential recurrences such as $T(n)=2T(n-1)$.

Foundation — used in: found.explog, found.series, dm.recurrence, algo.complexity, ga.quant.
cards.trap: Using simple interest where the question says compound, or adding the percentages (20% for 5 years is not 100%). Growth in year 2 is a percentage of the year 1 total, so use a power, not the product of $n$ and $r$.

scenes.title: Equal fractions on three strips of the same length

steps.caption: Cut a strip into 4 equal slices and shade 3. That is $\frac34$.
Cut an identical strip into 8 slices. The same shaded length covers 6 slices: $\frac68=\frac{3\times2}{4\times2}$.
Twelve slices: the same length covers 9, so $\frac9{12}=\frac{3\times3}{4\times3}$.
All three shaded bars end on the same line, so the three fractions are equal. Each came from multiplying top and bottom by the same number.
Backwards: divide top and bottom of $\frac9{12}$ by 3 and you are back at $\frac34$. That is simplifying.

scenes.title: Multiplying fractions as a fraction of a fraction of a rectangle

steps.caption: Cut a rectangle into 4 rows and 3 columns: 12 equal cells. The whole rectangle is 1.
Shade 3 of the 4 rows. That is $\frac34$ of the rectangle.
Now take 2 of the 3 columns. That is $\frac23$ **of** the shaded part.
The cells inside both outlines: $2\times3=6$ cells, out of 12 in total.
Multiply tops and bottoms: $\frac23\times\frac34=\frac{2\times3}{3\times4}=\frac6{12}=\frac12$.
A gets 2 parts and B gets 3 parts.
Count the equal parts in all: $2+3=5$.
One part is worth $90\div5=18$, so every part holds 18.
A has 2 parts: $2\times18=36$. B has 3 parts: $3\times18=54$.
Check: $36+54=90$, and $36:54$ reduces to $2:3$.

scenes.title: Inverse proportion: the same 36 painter-days, reshaped

steps.caption: Each cell is one painter-day of work. 4 painters for 9 days make a grid of 4 rows and 9 columns.
Count the cells: $4\times9=36$ painter-days of work in the job.
With 6 painters the job is still 36 cells. Reshape the same cells into 6 rows.
Columns: $36\div6=6$ days. More painters, fewer days: inverse proportion.

scenes.title: Percent as squares out of 100: 35% of 280

steps.caption: Percent means out of 100. The 100 squares make the whole: 100%.
35% is 35 squares out of 100: three full rows plus 5 squares. That is $\frac{35}{100}$.
Now the whole is 280. One square (1%) is worth $280\div100=2.8$.
35% of 280 is 35 squares worth 2.8 each: $35\times2.8=98$.
Reverse: 18 out of 60 is $\frac{18}{60}=0.30$, which fills 30 squares of 100. So 30%.

scenes.title: A 15% rise then a 15% fall does not return to the start

steps.caption: Start with a price of 400.
A rise of 15%: 15% of 400 is 60, so the price is 460. The multiplier is $1.15$.
Now a fall of 15% of the **new** price: 15% of 460 is 69, so $460-69=391$. The multiplier is $0.85$.
391 is below 400. The second 15% came from a bigger base, so it took away 69 while the first added only 60. Net: $\frac{391}{400}=0.9775$, a fall of 2.25%.
Start with 5000.
Year 2: 8% of the bigger 5400 is 432, so $5400\times1.08=5832$.
In one line: $5000\times1.08^3=6298.56$. Simple interest adds 400 each year and reaches only 6200. The extra 98.56 is interest on interest.
